## Email 1 — Mingda Li (mingda@mit.edu)

**Subject:** Collaboration Opportunity: AI-Powered Defect Engineering & Quantum Materials — BUAA ↔ MIT

Dear Professor Li,

I hope this message finds you well. I am Yuzhou Liu, Professor of Chemistry at Beihang University (Beijing) and founder of HeGuang ZhiCheng, an AI-driven materials design company. I recently read your groundbreaking 2026 *Nature Materials* paper on SCIGEN and your *Matter* work on the defect identification foundation model — both represent exactly the kind of "AI + physics" integration our group is pursuing.

At Beihang, we have built a GPU cluster (40×A100) coupled with in-situ characterization facilities (XPS, TEM, XAFS, synchrotron beamlines) focused on AI-driven catalyst and quantum materials discovery. Our recent work includes a universal GNN potential for heterogeneous catalysis (*Nature Computational Science*, 2025) and an autonomous catalysis lab that shortens development cycles by 60% (*Matter*, 2025).

I see strong synergy between your "defect foundation model" trained on 2,000 semiconductor vibrational spectra and our high-throughput experimental validation pipeline. Specifically, we would love to explore:

1. **Cross-validating your defect detection model** on our semiconductor/alloy sample library with neutron scattering + Raman data;
2. **Joint development of multi-modal AI** that fuses vibrational spectra with XAFS/TEM for universal defect quantification;
3. **Student/postdoc exchange** under a potential MIT-BUAA joint program.

Would you be open to a 30-minute virtual meeting in the coming weeks? We are also planning a "Joint Workshop on AI for Catalysis & Materials Design" at Beihang this fall (Sept–Nov 2026) and would be honored to host you as a keynote speaker.

Thank you for your time and for advancing the frontier of AI materials science.

Best regards,  
**Yuzhou Liu (刘宇宙)**  
Professor, School of Chemistry, Beihang University

**Subject:** Collaboration on Generative AI for Zeolite Synthesis + Sustainable Materials Lifecycle

Dear Professor Olivetti,

I am Yuzhou Liu, Professor at Beihang University's School of Chemistry and founder of HeGuang ZhiCheng, an AI materials startup in Beijing. Your 2026 *Nature Computational Science* paper on DiffSyn — using diffusion models trained on 23,000 synthesis recipes to plan zeolite synthesis — deeply resonated with our work. The "one-to-many" structure-to-synthesis mapping you addressed is precisely the bottleneck we face in scaling AI-designed catalysts to the lab.

Our group has developed an LLM-based materials synthesis knowledge extraction system (*npj Computational Materials*, 2025) that distills recipes from 500,000+ papers, and we are eager to integrate your diffusion-based generative approach. In parallel, our life-cycle assessment team (collaborating with Tsinghua's IE department) is building carbon-footprint databases for catalytic processes — directly complementary to your sustainability analytics.

We would welcome the opportunity to:

1. **Combine DiffSyn with our LLM synthesis database** to expand coverage beyond zeolites to MOFs and mixed-metal oxides;
2. **Co-develop an open-source synthesis planning benchmark** for the catalysis community;
3. **Host you at Beihang** this fall for a workshop on "AI for Sustainable Catalysis."

Would you be available for a brief video call to discuss these directions? We are enthusiastic about bridging MIT's generative modeling leadership with our experimental validation and industrialization capabilities in China.

Warm regards,  
**Yuzhou Liu (刘宇宙)**

**Subject:** Defect Foundation Models — Experimental Validation & Cross-Domain Transfer

Dear Mouyang,

Congratulations on your exceptional *Matter* paper (March 2026) presenting the defect identification foundation model using vibrational spectra! I am Yuzhou Liu, Professor at Beihang University. Your use of multi-head attention mechanisms to decode up to six simultaneous point defects from neutron scattering data is truly innovative — effectively bringing "ChatGPT-like" sequence modeling to materials characterization.

Our group at Beihang has accumulated Raman, XAFS, and neutron scattering data on ~3,000 catalytic and semiconductor samples, many with controlled defect concentrations (dopants, vacancies, interstitials). We believe this dataset could significantly extend your model's coverage beyond the 56 elements you reported, particularly into:

- **Transition metal oxides** (relevant to catalysis and batteries)
- **High-entropy alloys** with multi-principal-element defects
- **2D materials** (MoS₂, graphene derivatives) where defect engineering dominates properties

We would like to propose:

1. **Data sharing + model fine-tuning**: We contribute experimental spectra data to expand DefectNet, with co-authored follow-up paper;

3. **Joint workshop presentation**: We are organizing an "AI for Materials Characterization" session this fall and would love you to present.

As a rising leader in AI+materials, your perspective would be invaluable to our students. Would you be open to a call?

Best wishes,
